description_full: BK Technologies Corporation, through its subsidiary, BK Technologies, Inc., engages in the design, manufacture, and marketing of wireless communications products in the United States and internationally. It offers two-way land mobile radios (LMR) that are hand-held (portable) or installed in vehicles (mobile). The company offers KNG Series and BKR Series radios that operate in the P25 digital and analog modes, which are used primarily in government, public safety, military, and state and municipal government agencies, as well as various industrial and commercial enterprises; and BK radio products for intellectual property applications. In addition, it provides InteropONE, a push-to-talk-over-cellular (PTTOC) SaaS service that offers emergency incident commanders to establish group PTTOC between smartphone users directly from their smartphone. BK Technologies Corporation was incorporated in 1997 and is based in West Melbourne, Florida.
ceo_bio: Mr. John M. Suzuki | President, CEO & Director | Age 61 | Compensation: $631,789 (FY2025)
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 115 people. Revenue per employee of $749K ranks in the top quartile among Technology peers, improving at 10%/yr — growing workforce leverage. Each employee generates $160K of free cash flow annually. CEO compensation is 1× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags elevated compensation governance risk (9/10).
financial_summary: BK Technologies Corporation is a micro-cap technology business with a $252M market cap on $86M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +24% over the past three years and +11% annually across the full decade, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.
Returns on capital run at 6% against a 9% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests, with gross margins sitting at 49%.

The business throws off $18M in free cash flow — roughly 21 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.44× so those profits are backed by real cash.
Accruals are elevated at -9.3% of assets, and Sloan showed firms building earnings through accruals rather than cash systematically underperform.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year.
Shareholder yield is only 0.2%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 18% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is.

news_headlines.title: (BKTI) and the Role of Price-Sensitive Allocations

sect: Its 19% operating margin runs 12pp above the Technology median (7%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It earns less of the sector's profit than its revenue share would suggest (0.79x).
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+47.7% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 530 companies in the universe; the top four hold 29% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are roughly flat over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the bottom of its 52-week range, 36% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 46% and a beta of 0.85, it moves roughly with the market.
About $2.9M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 62% in the 2020 crash, 32% in the 2022 bear market and 85% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 41% below its DCF fair value of $113, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 13%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $89.67 to $146 (P10-P90).
On multiples it looks cheap against Technology peers: P/E 19.7 vs 26.7, EV/EBITDA 11.5 vs 16.4 and P/FCF 13.7 vs 25.4 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 30% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 7.3% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 7.5% (vs the 8% bar).
The Street target $97.00 on average, 45% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 6% falls short of the cost of capital of 9.0%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 2.74).
It runs a 49% gross margin and converts 21% of revenue into free cash flow, or -1% after stock compensation.
Earnings quality is mixed: cash conversion of 1.44x, but high accruals (-9.3% of assets).
ROE of 30% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.4x equity multiplier).
Operating margin is running 16pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
It spends 12.3% of revenue on R&D and 0.3% on stock compensation.
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $21.5M.
Its debt comes due soon (maturity wall about 0.5 years out), so refinancing terms matter.
Working capital ties up about 122 days of sales, a drag on cash generation.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 23.8% over 3 years, 14.3% over 5 years and 11.2% over 10 years, so growth is accelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 26%).
At current returns, reinvesting 100% of profits supports about 6.0% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 39.4% a year over five years.
Capex runs only 0.6x depreciation (1.2% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
own: Insiders own 18.5%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 59%.
Shareholder yield is a modest 0.2% (0.2% in buybacks).
The share count has grown 2.3% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
people: With about 115 employees, each generates about $749K of revenue, 2.0x the Technology median, and productivity has risen 9.5% a year.
That works out to $160K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $632K (1x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores poorly (9/10, lower is better).
